body.text: The Quad leaders – U.S. President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – are putting political differences aside to solve the urgent strategic risk presented by China’s critical mineral monopoly.

With the leaders’ meeting in Manila on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit, Quad nations are coordinating their critical mineral investment, regulations, and recycling to diversify from China and protect critical inputs to AI, defense, and energy. During his remarks after the summit, Trump said that the partners had “signed several new and critical rare earth trade deals to secure supply chains and ensure none of us become vulnerable to coercion by a single foreign supplier.”
The Quad Leaders’ Summit was a welcome sign after India-U.S. relations plunged last year.

In mid-2025, Trump applied a 50 percent tariff rate to India to penalize it for importing Russian oil while Moscow waged war in Ukraine. Around the same time, the Quad Foreign Ministers launched the Quad Critical Minerals Initiative in Washington DC.

The announcement added to an already bloated Quad agenda and conjured memories of the Quad falling short on other commitments, including providing a billion COVID-19 vaccines to the Indo-Pacific region. Moreover, tackling the complex market and technical challenges associated with critical mineral supply chains was ambitious, even for wealthier and more established groups, like the G7 Critical Minerals Alliance.

Skepticism around the Quad’s ability to deliver on a critical minerals agenda is warranted. A recent United States Studies Centre dialogue that brought together senior officials and private sector stakeholders from Quad countries revealed areas of convergence as well as divergence in national mineral priorities and expectations. But the Quad is the most likely minilateral framework to address this strategic chokepoint.

The Quad nations have advantages when it comes to creating mineral supply chains that route around China. Following China’s 2023 export restrictions on gallium and rare earths, Australia, the United States, and Japan leveraged their combined capital and offtake to back alternate Australian supply.

Notably, they have invested in the Alcoa-Sojitz gallium recovery facility in Western Australia, which is expected to supply 10 percent of global gallium. Bilaterally, Japan and Australia have joint offtake from Lynas Rare Earths and the United States and Australia have jointly invested in Arafura and Australian Strategic Materials.

Adding India to the critical mineral equation brings complication but also opportunity. Although the sixth largest economy in the world, India is still a developing country. While India lacks existing capacity, it has huge potential to support allied critical mineral supply chains. Where Australia brings raw ores and mining expertise, Japan brings manufacturing and technical expertise, and the U.S. brings capital and market power, India’s advantages will be in processing, recycling and manufacturing.

The additional benefit the Quad has over other mineral groupings is that the United States – with the most capital, inertia, and motivation – is driving this initiative. The Quad Critical Minerals Initiative was launched by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and follows a baked-in trend of Washington moving to secure minerals.

During his first term, Trump established the first U.S. critical minerals list to identify which minerals to protect. Critical minerals – along with energy – is a first order, enduring priority for the Trump administration. The focus on restoring critical mineral access will be sustained not only over Trump’s remaining two years but the next few U.S. presidencies.
The United States also has the deepest pockets and willingness to spend on mineral projects.

Since Trump’s inauguration last year, the U.S. government has committed or conditionally committed more than $27 billion to critical mineral projects, mostly in the United States but also in Australia. At a time when the U.S. government is fixated on “America first,” billion-dollar commitments to Australian miners show the U.S. is willing to spend its treasure abroad to solve this problem.

Lastly, other critical mineral groupings like the G7 Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance – launched by Canada and formalized by France – face political difficulties. Poor Canada-U.S. relations limit what the G7 framework can currently achieve.

Next year, the G7 presidency transitions from France to the U.S. and the Trump administration is unlikely to prioritize G7 critical minerals cooperation over the Quad or its bilateral FORGE (Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement) initiative.

At a time when confidence in global institutions is low and minilaterals are multiplying, some strategic groups will coalesce while others wane. The Quad itself has waxed and waned depending on individual members’ exposure to risk and their strategic alignment.

On critical minerals however, Quad nations are acutely at risk and have strong strategic alignment. Moreover, the minerals challenge is one that eclipses individual Quad leaders’ relations and long-term trends mean locked-in U.S. commitment. This makes the Quad the most likely framework to diversify critical mineral supply and still the most promising group on the world stage.
